0065 | \begin{abstract}
0066 | 
0067 |     We study high dimensional expansion beyond simplicial complexes (posets) and focus on $q$-complexes which are complexes whose basic building blocks are linear spaces. We show that the complete $q$-complex (consists of all subspaces of a given linear space) may have non-trivial homology groups and therefore some techniques for simplicial complexes fail. We develop new techniques to work bypass this. In particular:
0068 | 
0069 |     \begin{enumerate}
0070 |         \item We describe a new construction of cones and use it to determine when the homology of the complete $q$-complex is trivial. We use this construction to prove the ''projective support dimension conjecture'' conjectured by Mnukhin and Siemons \cite{MNUKHIN}.
0071 | 
0072 |         \item We define topological high dimensional expansion for posets, and show that the complete $q$-complex has linear (in the number of lines) coboundary expansion.
0073 | 
0074 |         \item We define the $q$-Linial-Meshulam model of random $q$ complexes and prove a sharp threshold for the connectivity of random $q$-complexes.
0075 |     \end{enumerate}
0076 | \end{abstract}
0077 | 
0078 | 
0079 | \section{Introduction}
0080 | 
0081 | In recent years, a theory of ''high dimensional expanders'' has emerged, and been successfully applied in mathematics and computer science to resolve longstanding open problems (\cite{LTCPaper}, \cite{LogConcave}). Another thread of research is using the geometry of vector spaces to obtain better construction in TCS, most notably, in the seminal works  \cite{UGC3}, \cite{UGC2} a weaker variant of the unique games conjecture was reduced to an expansion problem on the Grassmann graph which was later solved in \cite{UGC1}. The Grassmann graph is a graph whose vertices are the $\ell$ dimensional linear spaces of some $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ and two subspaces $U, W$ are connected by an edge if $dim(U \cap W)=\ell-1$.
fields.witness: Let V=F₃² and q(x,y)=x²+y². Its polar form is B((x,y),(u,v))=2xu+2yv, with matrix diag(2,2) and determinant 1 in F₃, so B is nondegenerate. Yet every nonzero square in F₃ equals 1: vectors with one nonzero coordinate have q=1, and those with two have q=2. Thus q has no nonzero isotropic vector.
